questions.q: What does the MATCH function return on its own?
options: The position of a value within a range, not the value itself
The actual value found at a position
The sum of all matching values
A #REF! error, always
questions.explain: MATCH only returns a position number — you need INDEX to actually fetch the value stored at that position.

questions.q: In =INDEX(ReturnColumn, MATCH(id, IDColumn, 0)), what does the 0 mean?
options: Exact match — the same concept as VLOOKUP's FALSE argument
Return the first row regardless of match
Round the result to zero decimal places
Search only empty cells
questions.explain: MATCH's third argument, match_type, set to 0 means exact match — functionally equivalent to passing FALSE as VLOOKUP's range_lookup argument.

questions.q: Why can INDEX/MATCH look left just as easily as XLOOKUP?
options: The lookup column (inside MATCH) and the return column (inside INDEX) are completely independent ranges, with no requirement that they be adjacent or in any order
INDEX/MATCH cannot look left — only XLOOKUP can
MATCH automatically reverses the direction of the search
INDEX only works on the leftmost column of a sheet
questions.explain: Because INDEX's return range and MATCH's lookup range are separate arguments, neither has to be positioned relative to the other — the same structural reason XLOOKUP can look left.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why does INDEX/MATCH still matter even though XLOOKUP exists?
options: It works in every Excel version back to the 1990s, unlike XLOOKUP which requires Excel 365/2021+, and it's common in workbooks built before 2019
INDEX/MATCH is always faster than XLOOKUP in every workbook
XLOOKUP was discontinued by Microsoft
INDEX/MATCH is required for formulas involving text
questions.explain: Version compatibility and the sheer number of pre-2019 workbooks still in circulation are the two concrete, practical reasons INDEX/MATCH fluency still matters.

questions.q: What capability does nesting a second MATCH inside INDEX unlock, covered fully in the next lesson?
options: A two-way lookup — finding a value at the intersection of a specific row and column
Automatically formatting the result as currency
Searching across multiple workbooks at once
Converting text to numbers automatically
questions.explain: MATCH can find a position in a row just as easily as a column, so nesting one MATCH for the row and one for the column lets INDEX pull a value from their intersection — a true two-way lookup.
